I've been building my own computer for a bit now, but it refused to boot up when I put everything together. Everything spins up fine, for the most part. The CPU fan runs, the RAM's lights turn on, the HDD even spins. The problem is the case fan won't budge, and the computer won't actually load anything from the HDD. It just kind of spins idly.

I've done every diagnostic test I can reasonably manage: I swapped out the PSU, checked the monitor, used both the new and old SATA connectors on the storage, pulled out the RAM and booted there (Mobo has no speaker, so I don't hear a POST), tried booting without an HDD, pulled the entire setup out of the case and tried breadboxing. Nothing. The case fan sits still until I power off the PSU- then it spins for a second and stops.

It's not a complicated build. I have a WD 1 TB HDD, a Ryzen 3 2200g, dual Corsair Vengence 3000 mhz 8 gb RAM, an ASRock Fatal1ty AB350 mini itx/ac,, and an insignia 450 watt power supply. As it stands, I think the Mobo is DOA, but I could use some input from someone else.

If it's failing to even make an audible post beep then the system itself isn't successfully loading the BIOS.

Remove the CMOS battery for 30 seconds and re-seat. Then, jump the CMOS jumper. Attempt to boot.

If the same symptoms happen (fans spin a moment then stop, no post boot beep) then the motherboard is DOA.

Could be the pin out from the motherboard to the case, usb pin outs can also be a problem. Sometime just unseating the cpu and plugging it back in can fix it. Different lights flashing on the front could also give a clue to your problem. Could be bad part. Could be underpowered if you a have ton of stuff plugged in start unplugging things. Even mouse and keyboard can cause issues.
I can't plug the Mobo to the case's front. Mismatched power pins. I've been shorting it on so far. As for the rest, I tried it all, sadly.
450W seems low for a modern desktop. Are you sure the rails for your CPU and motherboard have enough capacity?

I think you missed the point. If you have a rail that does 10A and you put everything on it, you get 120W total to work with, even if you have unused ones that can support the rest.

Lower watt power supply means more likely to encounter this problem.

I don't know if this is op's psu, but here is the output for an insignia 450W psu.

i don't think that you would ever have a 12V rail as low as 10A, it wouldn't make sense at all. Can the 24 pin be supplied by 2 rails? i'm not sure.

I've seen some real weird splits on the rails. Some have a dedicated one just for motherboard and processor and one fan. With a new processor and onboard graphics you can totally overload some of those because they're usually older.

You're right that it looks like it's no issue here. Making a 24V rail from 2 12s in series would only work if they were isolated, which is unlikely to be the case.
you misread, i meant "could the 2 12V pins on the atx connector be fed off of 2 different rails?"

Assuming they share a common, it would almost always work, but if those pins are connected on the motherboard side you now have two switching circuits fighting for level control which will eventually burn out your power supply due to tiny differences in calibration and timing. I don't know enough about how the motherboard uses them to tell you what other risks you could face other than "probably some."
